speaker_role: independent counselor (nearly two decades as independent college consultant, also SAT/ACT coach)
commercial_incentive: yes -- explicitly promotes SupertutorTV's test-prep courses and channel subscription
key_insights: Argues published early vs. regular admit-rate gaps (e.g., Harvard ~7-8% early vs ~3.3% regular; Dartmouth ~22% early vs ~4.5% regular class of 2025) overstate any individual student's true probability boost from applying early
Students with weak/unfinished essays, especially for highly competitive schools, should not apply early; polishing the whole application matters more than timing

Students whose grades are on a strong upward trend, or whose senior-year course rigor is notably higher than prior years, may benefit from waiting since first impressions are hard to reverse once deferred
A 'wow factor' matters more for sub-5%-admit-rate top-10 schools than for schools ranked roughly 20-50, where GPA/scores/proficiency matter more

Three reasons early admit rates overstate probability: (1) many of the strongest applicants get 'plucked off' early and don't compete in the regular round, (2) legacy applicants are concentrated in early pools at schools like Penn/Harvard and are admitted at several times the base rate, (3) regular-round applicant pools swell with rejected-early students reapplying broadly, inflating apparent competition without proportional quality

The early-application advantage is argued to be smaller at the most selective schools (Harvard, Stanford) and larger at schools roughly ranked 15-50, where demonstrated yield commitment (especially via ED) carries more weight
specific_numbers_or_facts: Speaker cites Harvard early admit rate ~7-8% vs regular ~3.3%
Speaker cites Dartmouth Class of 2025 early admit rate ~22% vs regular ~4.5%
Speaker describes legacy admit rates as roughly four to five times a non-legacy applicant's rate
notable_or_distinctive: Goes beyond the common 'apply early, it helps' advice by explicitly deconstructing why published admit-rate gaps mislead individual applicants (self-selection of strong students, legacy concentration, and regular-pool reapplication dynamics).
reliability_notes: Figures are stated from memory/recollection without citing a source document, and admit rates cited are for specific past application cycles that may be outdated for current applicants; overall reasoning is coherent but the numbers should be independently verified.
